The Japanese butterfish Psenopsis anomala, a member of the medusafish family Centrolophidae, is a pelagic species distributed across the northwestern Pacific. Studies of landed catches and otolith-based age estimation indicate that fully grown, sexually mature adults attain an ultimate total length of 30 cm [Li = 30 cm]. The asymptotic body mass observed in these large, reproductively active individuals is about 484 grams [Wwi = about 484 grams] under natural conditions, a size consistent with the typical body plan of stromateoid fishes. This mass plateau is reached after several years of gradually decelerating growth, reflecting the trade-off between continued somatic investment and the onset of annual reproductive output in iteroparous adults. The species occupies mesopelagic waters where it feeds on gelatinous zooplankton, a diet that may limit maximal growth rates yet supports the accumulation of metabolic reserves necessary for the substantial reproductive investment observed in this iteroparous adult. Compared to the larger confamilial Hyperoglyphe antarctica, which attains lengths exceeding 60 cm, the ultimate dimensions of P. anomala are considerably more modest, reflecting its earlier maturation and shorter lifespan.

At the opposite end of the size spectrum, embryogenesis in Psenopsis anomala produces extremely small offspring. Following external fertilisation and a period of incubation, the chorion ruptures at eclosion, releasing a yolk-sac larva that is barely visible to the unaided eye. Measurements of newly hatched individuals indicate a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.00022 g [Wwb = approximately 0.00022 g]. This minuscule mass is characteristic of marine teleosts that produce large numbers of small, pelagic eggs, a strategy that disperses mortality risk across a vast larval cohort. Despite this tiny starting size, juveniles grow rapidly through the postflexion larval stage and proceed toward sexual maturation. Field surveys have documented that gonadal maturation is initiated when young fish reach a total length of about 15 cm [Lp = about 15 cm], marking the pubertal transition. This threshold represents a critical life-history shift, as energy that previously fuelled somatic growth is redirected toward gametogenesis and the development of secondary sexual characteristics. The relatively early maturation at this length suggests that P. anomala is capable of initiating reproductive activity well before attaining its asymptotic size, a life-history trait that buffers against environmental stochasticity affecting survival to large body size.

The reproductive output of Psenopsis anomala has been quantified under controlled thermal conditions designed to mimic the cool-temperate waters of its natural habitat. When maintained at a constant 18.4 °C [T = 18.4 °C], a temperature that falls within the optimal range for gonadal recrudescence in this species, reproductively active females produce a maximum daily egg output of approximately 192 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 192 eggs per day]. This prodigious daily reproductive output is typical of a broadcast-spawning iteroparous teleost that releases multiple pelagic egg batches across an extended spawning season. The prodigious egg production ensures that, despite extremely high mortality among larval stages, sufficient numbers of recruits successfully pass through the pelagic larval phase and undergo metamorphosis to replenish benthic juvenile populations. Comparative data suggest that centrolophid fishes generally partition reproductive effort into numerous small eggs rather than investing in a few large, well-provisioned offspring, a pattern consistent with the low per-offspring investment reflected in the tiny hatchling mass of P. anomala. Fecundity in this species scales with female body size, and the largest individuals approaching the ultimate length are responsible for the maximum reproductive rates.

Embryonic development rates in Psenopsis anomala are strongly temperature-dependent, as is typical for poikilothermic teleosts. When incubating fertilised ova are held at 18.4 °C [T = 18.4 °C], the period from syngamy to the completion of yolk-sac resorption and the onset of exogenous feeding occupies approximately 13.5 days [ab = approximately 13.5 days]. This relatively short developmental interval to first feeding is consistent with the small egg size and the warm-temperate thermal regime of the species' spawning grounds. During this time, the embryonated egg progresses through cleavage, blastulation, and gastrulation while consuming its yolk reserve, culminating in the secretion of chorionase enzymes that weaken the egg envelope and permit hatching. The resulting prolarva, still endowed with a substantial yolk sac, drifts as passive ichthyoplankton for an additional period before the onset of exogenous feeding and swim bladder inflation. The duration of this pre-feeding phase, although variable, is generally short in the centrolophids, with first prey capture occurring shortly after mouth gape opening and full absorption of the yolk. This timing aligns well with developmental schedules reported for confamilial medusafishes, although direct comparative data on embryonic durations in centrolophids remain sparse. Rapid embryogenesis at this temperature is thought to minimize the exposure of vulnerable early-life stages to predation, a selective pressure that likely shaped the reproductive strategy of P. anomala.

Longevity records for Psenopsis anomala derive primarily from captive rearing studies in which individuals were exposed to a stable thermal environment of 18.4 °C [T = 18.4 °C] throughout their post-settlement life. Under these conditions, the maximum documented lifespan reaches approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years], although most individuals in the wild are unlikely to survive beyond their third reproductive season due to predation, disease, and the cumulative cost of repeated spawning at a temperature of 18.4 °C [T = 18.4 °C]. Post-reproductive mortality in this species appears to rise steeply after the fourth year, with senescence characterized by a progressive decline in swimming performance and immune competence. The relatively modest lifespan of this butterfish contrasts with the longer lives of some larger centrolophids, such as Hyperoglyphe antarctica, yet remains sufficient to allow several annual breeding opportunities, thereby enhancing lifetime reproductive success. Otolith-based age validation in field-caught specimens has confirmed that the majority of the adult population falls within the 1–3 year age bracket, with only a small fraction reaching the 5-year maximum, a pattern of early actuarial senescence that aligns with life-history theory for small to medium-sized pelagic iteroparous teleosts under high natural predation pressure.
